did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm’s title says that it was intended for the music director, set to “The Lilies,” and attributed to Asaph; the word “Testimony” also appears in the title.
Did you know? The LORD is described here with two images and titles: “Shepherd of Israel,” who leads His people like a flock, and “You who are enthroned above the cherubim.”
Did you know? The verse mentions Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh together, and asks the LORD to stir up His might and come to save His people.

Did you know? The psalm gives a vivid description of suffering: the people eat “bread of tears” and drink tears, and they have become a source of strife to their neighbors and a mockery to their enemies.
Did you know? The request “O God of hosts, restore us” is repeated in the psalm, together with the plea for the LORD’s face to shine upon them, forming a refrain of supplication for salvation.

Did you know? Israel is compared to a vine that the LORD brought out of Egypt, drove out nations before, and planted in the land; this portrays the transition from slavery to being established in the land.
Did you know? The vine is described as spreading over a vast area: its branches reach the sea, and its shoots reach the River. The imagery emphasizes the extent of its growth.
Did you know? After the description of the great vine, the question is asked why its walls have been broken down, leaving it exposed to passersby and to those who would harm it.
Did you know? Among those harming the vine are “the boar from the forest” and “the creatures of the field”; these animals represent the forces that attack the vine.
Did you know? The psalm ends by repeating the plea, “LORD God of hosts, restore us,” followed by a request for the LORD’s face to shine upon them and save them.
